## Introduction

In this tutorial you will build a small **website** about the history of Major League Baseball. You will use AI to do the analysis and the **[Lahman](https://cran.r-project.org/package=Lahman)** baseball database as your data source. Your job is to steer the analysis, render often, inspect the output, and write the words that turn a few charts into a page worth reading.

###

Use AI however you like.

You should be doing this tutorial in a repo named `baseball`. If you are not, create one and then connect to it. You may need to restart this tutorial after you do so.

In this repo, create a new Quarto **website** project, as you did in the Websites tutorials. The project should include a `_quarto.yml` configuration file and a home page named `index.qmd`. Give the site the title `"Baseball"`. Quarto also creates an `about.qmd` page and a `styles.css` file: delete both, and remove the lines that mention them from `_quarto.yml`, so the site starts with just the home page.

In a bash Terminal, render the whole site:


Quarto builds the site into a `_site` directory. Open `_site/index.html` with Live Server (right-click it in the Explorer → **Open with Live Server**) and keep the tab open. It refreshes every time you render. Going forward, we will just tell you to "Render" when we want you to take these steps.

Make sure your `.gitignore` ignores the generated site and Quarto's intermediate files, each entry on its own line:



###

A Quarto website is a *project*: `quarto render` builds every `.qmd` in the folder into a linked set of HTML pages under `_site/`. That output is generated, so it does not belong in your repo --- `.gitignore` keeps `_site/`, the `.quarto/` working directory, and the per-page `_files/` figure directories out of git, leaving only your source.

## Home runs

Major League Baseball has kept detailed records since 1871, and the **Lahman** database packages that history for R. Its `Teams` table holds one row per team per season; its `Batting` table holds one row per player per season. We start with the home run --- the sport's signature event --- and a puzzle hiding in plain sight.

```{r}
Teams
```

###

`Teams` has 48 columns and one row for every team in every season since 1871 --- the unit of observation is a *team-season*. For finer detail, analysts reach for **Retrosheet** (play-by-play for every game) or **Statcast** (pitch-by-pitch tracking since 2015, available in R through the **[baseballr](https://billpetti.github.io/baseballr/)** package); Lahman is the right grain for questions about whole seasons.

### Exercise 2

That table is too wide to read, and we need only three of its 48 columns: `yearID`, the season; `G`, games played (about 162 in a modern full season); and `HR`, that team's home runs. Change the chunk to add up all teams' home runs and all teams' games within each season, producing a table with one row per season holding the total home runs and the total team-games.

Render. In the R Terminal, run `show_file("home-runs.qmd")`.

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: home-runs-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "That table is too wide to read, and we need only three of its 48 columns: yearID, the season; G, games played (about 162 in a modern full season); and HR, that team's home runs. Change the chunk to add up all teams' home runs and all teams' games within each season, producing a table with one row per season holding the total home runs and the total team-games. Render. In the R Terminal, run show_file(\"home-runs.qmd\"). CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: home-runs-3-answer
#| echo: true
Teams |>
  group_by(yearID) |>
  summarise(HR = sum(HR, na.rm = TRUE),
            team_games = sum(G),
            .groups = "drop")
```

###

Now the unit of observation is a *season*: one row per year, from 1871 to 2025. We use `na.rm = TRUE` because one 1932 team --- the Negro Southern League's Columbus Turf Club, which played only 10 games --- has no home run total in the source data.

### Exercise 3

Plot total home runs by season as a line. Aggregate the home runs per year inside the chunk and put `yearID` on the x-axis and total home runs on the y-axis. Give it a title, axis labels, and a source caption.

Render. Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below. To take a screenshot, press `Cmd + Ctrl + Shift + 4` on a Mac, `Win + Shift + S` on Windows, or `Ctrl + Shift + Show windows` on a Chromebook, select the area, then click in the answer box and press `Cmd + V` (Mac) or `Ctrl + V` (Windows) to paste it.

```{r}
#| label: home-runs-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Plot total home runs by season as a line. Aggregate the home runs per year inside the chunk and put yearID on the x-axis and total home runs on the y-axis. Give it a title, axis labels, and a source caption. Render. Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: home-runs-4-answer
#| echo: true
Teams |>
  group_by(yearID) |>
  summarise(HR = sum(HR, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = yearID, y = HR)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 0.7, color = "navy") +
  labs(
    title = "Total home runs per season, with some puzzling collapses",
    subtitle = "Major League Baseball, 1871-2025",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Total home runs",
    caption = "Source: Lahman Teams table"
  )
```

###

The long climb makes sense: more teams, more games, and a livelier game all push the total up. But look at the sudden cliffs: in 2020 the total crashes to about 2,300 home runs --- a level last seen in the 1950s --- and there are sharp dips in 1981 and 1994 too.

### Exercise 4

Investigate those collapses. Build a small table comparing a normal recent season (2019) with the three suspicious ones (1981, 1994, 2020), showing each season's total home runs, total team-games, and home runs per game.

Render. In the R Terminal, run `show_file("home-runs.qmd")`.

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: home-runs-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Investigate those collapses. Build a small table comparing a normal recent season (2019) with the three suspicious ones (1981, 1994, 2020), showing each season's total home runs, total team-games, and home runs per game. Render. In the R Terminal, run show_file(\"home-runs.qmd\"). CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: home-runs-5-answer
#| echo: true
Teams |>
  group_by(yearID) |>
  summarise(HR = sum(HR, na.rm = TRUE),
            team_games = sum(G),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(hr_per_game = HR / team_games) |>
  filter(yearID %in% c(2019, 1981, 1994, 2020))
```

###

In 2020 the season was cut to 60 games by the COVID-19 pandemic --- about 1,800 team-games instead of the usual 4,860 --- so the *total* fell even though the *rate* was 1.28 home runs per game, near an all-time high. 1981 and 1994 were strike-shortened seasons: the dips were never about hitting; they were about how many games got played.

### Exercise 5

Redo the plot using home runs per game instead of the total: divide each season's total home runs by its total team-games, and plot that rate against the season. Keep a title, labels, and caption.

Render. Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: home-runs-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Redo the plot using home runs per game instead of the total: divide each season's total home runs by its total team-games, and plot that rate against the season. Keep a title, labels, and caption. Render. Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: home-runs-6-answer
#| echo: true
Teams |>
  group_by(yearID) |>
  summarise(HR = sum(HR, na.rm = TRUE),
            team_games = sum(G),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(hr_per_game = HR / team_games) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = yearID, y = hr_per_game)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 0.7, color = "navy") +
  labs(
    title = "Home runs per game reveal baseball's real eras",
    subtitle = "MLB home runs per team per game, 1871-2025",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Home runs per game",
    caption = "Source: Lahman Teams table"
  )
```

###

The artifact dips are gone, and the real story appears. The rate sits near zero through the **dead-ball era** before 1920, jumps sharply in the 1920s (Babe Ruth, a livelier ball, and a ban on the spitball), sags during World War II as players left for military service, climbs through the late-1990s and 2000s **steroid era**, and spikes to a record 1.39 in 2019 --- the season of the so-called "juiced ball."

### Exercise 6

Polish the plot. Flag the shortened seasons --- 1918, 1919, 1981, 1994, 1995, and 2020 --- in a different color so a reader can see that the very seasons that fooled us earlier are ordinary once we use a rate. Add a legend and update the labels.

Render. Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: home-runs-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Polish the plot. Flag the shortened seasons (1918, 1919, 1981, 1994, 1995, and 2020) in a different color so a reader can see that the very seasons that fooled us earlier are ordinary once we use a rate. Add a legend and update the labels. Render. Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: home-runs-7-answer
#| echo: true
Teams |>
  group_by(yearID) |>
  summarise(HR = sum(HR, na.rm = TRUE),
            team_games = sum(G),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(hr_per_game = HR / team_games,
         shortened = yearID %in% c(1918, 1919, 1981, 1994, 1995, 2020)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = yearID, y = hr_per_game)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(aes(color = shortened), size = 1.1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(`FALSE` = "navy", `TRUE` = "red"),
    labels = c("Full season", "Shortened season"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Home runs per game reveal baseball's real eras",
    subtitle = "MLB home runs per team per game, 1871-2025",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Home runs per game",
    caption = "Source: Lahman Teams table"
  )
```

###

The red points sit right on the trend line: once we measure a rate, the strike and pandemic years are unremarkable. This is the payoff of the whole section --- the same seasons that looked like collapses in the first plot are now visibly normal.

###

Home runs per game is one of the cleanest ways to see baseball's history in a single line, but a rate hides who produced it. The 2019 spike and the late-1990s climb were the work of specific players, and the league total says nothing about whether many hitters improved a little or a few improved enormously --- a distinction any aggregate measure buries.

## Sluggers

The league trend is made of individual careers. The **Lahman** `Batting` table records every player's batting line for every season, and the `People` table holds their names and biographical details. We will find the career home run leaders and connect them back to the eras we just discovered.

### Exercise 1

Create a new page named `sluggers.qmd`, giving it the title `"Sluggers"`, and add it to the navbar in `_quarto.yml` with the same label.

At the top of the page, add a code chunk that loads `library(tidyverse)` and `library(Lahman)` with `#| message: false`. `Batting` has about 128,000 rows --- one per player per season per team, going back to 1871 --- so a player who batted for fifteen seasons contributes roughly fifteen rows. In a second chunk, add up each player's home runs across all of their seasons, and show the 15 players with the most career home runs.

Render. In the R Terminal, run `show_file("sluggers.qmd")`.

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: sluggers-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Create a new page named sluggers.qmd, giving it the title \"Sluggers\", and add it to the navbar in _quarto.yml with the same label. At the top of the page, add a code chunk that loads library(tidyverse) and library(Lahman) with #| message: false. Batting has about 128,000 rows (one per player per season per team, going back to 1871), so a player who batted for fifteen seasons contributes roughly fifteen rows. In a second chunk, add up each player's home runs across all of their seasons, and show the 15 players with the most career home runs. Render. In the R Terminal, run show_file(\"sluggers.qmd\"). CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: sluggers-2-answer
#| echo: true
Batting |>
  group_by(playerID) |>
  summarise(HR = sum(HR, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(HR, n = 15)
```

###

The counts are right, but the players are unreadable: `bondsba01` is a `playerID`, not a name. Lahman splits its data across tables --- batting in one, biographical details in another --- and joins them on `playerID`.

### Exercise 2

Join the `People` table to attach each leader's name. Build a clean table showing the player's full name, their career home run total, and the span of seasons they played (first year to last year).

Render. In the R Terminal, run `show_file("sluggers.qmd")`.

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: sluggers-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Join the People table to attach each leader's name. Build a clean table showing the player's full name, their career home run total, and the span of seasons they played (first year to last year). Render. In the R Terminal, run show_file(\"sluggers.qmd\"). CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: sluggers-3-answer
#| echo: true
Batting |>
  group_by(playerID) |>
  summarise(HR = sum(HR, na.rm = TRUE),
            first = min(yearID),
            last = max(yearID),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(HR, n = 15) |>
  left_join(People, by = "playerID") |>
  mutate(player = paste(nameFirst, nameLast),
         span = paste0(first, "-", last)) |>
  select(player, HR, span)
```

###

Barry Bonds leads with 762, ahead of Hank Aaron (755) and Babe Ruth (714). Look at the career spans: several of these players were active in the same window, which is the thread we pull on next.

```{r}
learnr2::question(
  "Turn the leaders into a bar chart. Put career home runs on the x-axis and player names on the y-axis, ordered so the leader is on top, and color the bars by whether each player was active during the steroid era. Treat a player as active in that era if their career overlapped the years 1994 to 2009 (their last season was 1994 or later and their first season was 2009 or earlier). Add a legend, a title, labels, and a caption. Render. Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: sluggers-5-answer
#| echo: true
Batting |>
  group_by(playerID) |>
  summarise(HR = sum(HR, na.rm = TRUE),
            first = min(yearID),
            last = max(yearID),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(HR, n = 15) |>
  left_join(People, by = "playerID") |>
  mutate(player = paste(nameFirst, nameLast),
         steroid_era = last >= 1994 & first <= 2009) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = HR, y = fct_reorder(player, HR), fill = steroid_era)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(`FALSE` = "grey65", `TRUE` = "navy"),
    labels = c("No", "Yes"),
    name = "Active 1994-2009"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Most career home run leaders played in the steroid era",
    subtitle = "Top 15 in MLB history",
    x = "Career home runs",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Lahman Batting and People tables"
  )
```

###

Nine of the top fifteen were active between 1994 and 2009 --- the same window where the per-game rate on the previous page climbed to its modern peak. That is not a coincidence: Bonds, Sosa, McGwire, Rodriguez, and Palmeiro all played in an era later marked by performance-enhancing drug scandals.

### Exercise 4

Zoom in on the career home run leader, Barry Bonds. Plot his home runs in each season of his career as a bar chart, with season on the x-axis. Add a title and labels.

Render. Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: sluggers-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Zoom in on the career home run leader, Barry Bonds. Plot his home runs in each season of his career as a bar chart, with season on the x-axis. Add a title and labels. Render. Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: sluggers-6-answer
#| echo: true
Batting |>
  filter(playerID == "bondsba01") |>
  group_by(yearID) |>
  summarise(HR = sum(HR), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = yearID, y = HR)) +
  geom_col(fill = "navy") +
  labs(
    title = "Barry Bonds hit more home runs in his late 30s than ever before",
    subtitle = "Home runs per season; the 73 in 2001 is still the single-season record",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Home runs",
    caption = "Source: Lahman Batting table"
  )
```

###

Most hitters peak in their late twenties and decline. Bonds did the opposite: his biggest seasons came after age 35, capped by a record 73 home runs in 2001.

Two pages, two units of observation: the home runs page counts seasons, the sluggers page counts careers. Keeping each page to one grain is what makes a multi-page site easier to read than one long document --- a reader always knows what a row means.

## Summary

This tutorial used AI to build a multi-page website about Major League Baseball history with the **Lahman** database. You discovered why total home runs appear to collapse in shortened seasons, normalized to home runs per game to expose the sport's real eras, and ranked the career home run leaders --- connecting nine of the top fifteen back to the steroid-era spike in the league rate.

###

```{.output}
---
title: "Baseball"
---

## Welcome

This site explores the history of Major League Baseball through the
Lahman database, a record of every team and player season since 1871.

The **Home runs** page starts with a puzzle: total home runs seem to
collapse in 1981, 1994, and 2020. The collapse is an illusion of
shortened seasons --- measured per game, those years are ordinary, and
the rate instead reveals baseball's real eras, from the dead-ball era to
the 2019 "juiced ball." The **Sluggers** page ranks the career home run
leaders and finds most of them clustered in the steroid era, the same
years the per-game rate peaked.
```

###

A website's landing page is where a visitor decides whether to keep reading. Stating the findings up front --- and pointing to the pages that back them up --- is what makes a collection of charts feel like one coherent project.
